headline: New Hampshire revenues beat September plan as business taxes set a record
dek: General and Education Fund receipts ran $69.1 million above the monthly target, giving the state a stronger-than-expected start to fiscal 2027 while budget questions remain.
body: New Hampshire's General Fund and Education Trust Fund revenues exceeded the state's September plan by $69.1 million, according to the monthly report released by the Department of Administrative Services. The result gives Gov. Kelly Ayotte's administration a stronger opening to fiscal 2027, but one month of receipts does not settle the state's longer-term budget outlook. Ayotte highlighted the results in a statement released Oct. 5.

The biggest driver was business taxation. New Hampshire collected $269.8 million in business tax revenue during September, surpassing the previous September record of $226.4 million set in 2024, the state's report says. The comparison is with September collections, not with a full fiscal-year total, and the report does not by itself identify how much of the increase came from business performance, filing timing, or other changes in the tax base.

For the first three months of fiscal 2027, the state says combined General Fund and Education Trust Fund revenues were $74.9 million, or 12.5%, above plan. Collections were also $111.7 million higher than at the same point a year earlier. Those are useful measures of the budget's current position, but they remain preliminary. The monthly report will be revised as additional receipts are recorded and as the state compares actual collections with its formal revenue estimates.

New Hampshire relies heavily on business taxes and other relatively narrow revenue sources because it does not levy a broad personal income tax or general sales tax. That structure can make individual payment months especially important to the budget. It also means that a strong month should be read alongside the composition of the receipts, not just the headline surplus. A high business-tax month can improve the state's near-term cash position without guaranteeing that the same pace will continue through the fiscal year.

The state's recent history offers a reason for caution. In a September analysis published by the [New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute](https://nhfpi.org/columns/state-revenues-end-fiscal-year-higher-but-sources-of-growth-raise-questions-for-the-next-budget-new-hampshire-business-review/), the institute said fiscal 2026 collections in the two funds finished $170 million above budget writers' target. It reported that about $98.8 million, or 58.1% of that surplus, came from a one-time tax-amnesty program. That earlier example does not explain September's new results, but it shows why policymakers distinguish recurring revenue growth from temporary or unusual receipts.

The latest numbers are therefore a fiscal signal rather than a new spending authorization. They may give lawmakers and state agencies more room as they monitor the fiscal 2027 budget, but the report does not announce a tax cut, a new program, or a change to the adopted spending plan. Any such decisions would require separate action through the governor and Legislature, and the revenue report does not predict what they will do.

The numbers also matter beyond Concord because state revenue helps support statewide education and other public services while local governments remain reliant on property taxes for much of their own spending. A sustained revenue gain could ease pressure on the state budget, but it would not automatically reduce municipal tax bills or guarantee more money for a particular school district. Those effects would depend on later budget decisions and the distribution of state aid.

For now, the clearest conclusion is that New Hampshire entered the new fiscal year ahead of its revenue plan, led by an unusually strong September for business taxes. The important unanswered question is whether that performance reflects durable economic activity or a timing effect concentrated in one reporting period. The next monthly revenue releases will show whether the margin narrows, holds, or grows as fiscal 2027 develops.
